The fanshell (Cyprogenia stegaria) is a critically imperiled freshwater mussel native to river systems of the eastern United States, where it depends on specific host fish to complete its parasitic larval stage. At the moment of release from the female's brood chamber, the larval glochidium measures just 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters] in shell length, an extraordinarily small size typical of unionoid bivalves that produce fully formed but microscopic larvae rather than free-swimming veligers. Following a period of encystment on the gills or fins of a suitable host fish, the glochidium metamorphoses and drops off as a free-living juvenile, settling into the streambed at a shell length at settlement of only 0.03 centimeters . At a water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the age at birth reaches approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], reflecting the encystment period required before the juvenile mussel becomes independent of its host.

Once settled, the post-metamorphic juvenile begins a prolonged phase of somatic growth, burrowing into the substrate and filter-feeding on suspended particulate matter. Growth continues over many years as the mussel accumulates shell material and soft tissue mass, a slow process typical of long-lived unionids inhabiting stable riverine gravel beds. The species eventually reaches the size threshold associated with reproductive capability, attaining a shell length at puberty of 3 centimeters [Lp = 3 centimeters], a milestone that marks the onset of gametogenesis after several years of benthic growth.

The ultimate shell length attained by fully grown adults of Cyprogenia stegaria reaches 5.6 centimeters [Li = 5.6 centimeters], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 6.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.3 grams]. This modest asymptotic size is typical of the smaller unionid mussels and reflects the species' preference for swift-flowing, well-oxygenated riffle habitats where large body size may confer little advantage against dislodgement by current. Reaching this maximum size requires sustained growth over a substantial fraction of the species' total lifespan.

Longevity in Cyprogenia stegaria is considerable for a freshwater bivalve of its modest body size, with a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years] at the same reference temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This extended lifespan allows individuals to participate in multiple reproductive events across many years, a demographic buffer that is especially important given the species' complete dependence on a compatible host fish for larval development. The combination of a tiny 0.02-centimeter larva (0.02 centimeters) [Lb = 0.02 centimeters] and a 5.6-centimeter adult shell (5.6 centimeters) [Li = 5.6 centimeters] illustrates the substantial growth trajectory that this imperiled mussel must complete within the constraints of its increasingly fragmented riverine habitat.
